title: Rohit Yadav Finishes Seventh as India Claims Javelin Silver and Bronze at Glasgow
excerpt: Neeraj Chopra took silver and debutant Yashvir Singh earned a personal-best bronze behind Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga, while Rohit Yadav's 81.56m fell short of his 87.05m national form.
body:
• Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga won gold with 89.75m; Neeraj Chopra took silver at 85.83m and Yashvir Singh bronze at 85.41m (personal best)
  • Rohit Yadav finished seventh with 81.56m, well below his 87.05m personal best set at the national championships
  • All three Indian javelin throwers made the 12-man final — a first in Commonwealth Games history
  • Pakistan's Arshad Nadeem, the reigning Olympic champion, finished ninth with 77.41m

Tharanga Stuns the Field

Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga produced the throw of the evening in round two — a massive 89.75m that no one could match across five subsequent rounds. The world leader this season, Tharanga had topped qualification at 82.84m and entered the final as favourite. He delivered, winning Sri Lanka's first-ever Commonwealth javelin gold.

Neeraj Chopra, competing in his first Commonwealth Games since 2018 after missing the 2022 Birmingham edition through injury, managed a season-best 85.83m in the second round to secure silver. The Olympic and world champion had been managing a lower back injury since September 2025 and entered Glasgow with limited competition behind him — just one outing at the Doha Diamond League in June, where he finished fourth with 85.69m.

Yashvir Singh's Breakout Moment

The surprise of the final was Yashvir Singh's sixth-round throw of 85.41m, a personal best that vaulted him from outside the medal positions to bronze. The Rajasthan thrower had qualified in tenth place and showed composure under pressure when it mattered most, saving his best for the final attempt.

Grenada's Anderson Peters, a two-time world champion, finished fourth at 83.88m, while South Africa's Douw Smit and Trinidad's Keshorn Walcott completed the top six.

Rohit Yadav's Quiet Night

Rohit Yadav had arrived in Glasgow riding a wave of form. At the National Inter-State Championships in Bhubaneswar earlier this year, the 25-year-old from Uttar Pradesh had launched a stunning 87.05m — his final-attempt throw that made him only the third Indian to clear 87 metres, after Neeraj Chopra and Kishore Jena.

"I've been crossing distances of 86m and 87m in practice but I couldn't translate those throws during competitions. It was hurting me badly."

— Rohit Yadav, after his 87.05m national record

But that translation problem resurfaced at Glasgow. Rohit's best of 81.56m came in the second round, and he could not improve across four more attempts. His series of 77.50, 81.56, foul, 73.70, foul, and 79.55 reflected the inconsistency he himself has acknowledged.

Still, Rohit's story is one of perseverance. Born in Dabhiya village near Jaunpur, his father — a farmer and former decathlete — could not afford a proper javelin and began cutting them from wild bamboo to train Rohit and his two younger brothers. An elbow ligament injury in 2023 cost him an entire season, including the 2024 Olympics.

India's Javelin Depth on Display

The bigger narrative from Glasgow is India's javelin depth. Having all three throwers advance to a 12-man Commonwealth final is unprecedented, and the silver-bronze finish — combined with Rohit's presence in the top eight — signals a program that extends well beyond Neeraj Chopra alone.

Notably, Pakistan's Arshad Nadeem, who won Olympic gold in Paris with a massive 92.97m, had a quiet evening in Glasgow. The reigning champion managed just 77.41m and was eliminated after three rounds, finishing ninth.

What's Next

Chopra will turn his attention to the 2026 Asian Games, while Rohit and Yashvir will look to build on this experience. For Rohit, the challenge remains bridging the gap between training throws and competition performance — a gap that, when closed, could put him among the world's best.
